articles.title: Frevo between Street and Institution: Transmission, Urban Space, and Cultural Policy in Recife and Olinda
articles.abstract: This article examines how frevo—the high-energy music-dance tradition of Pernambuco—navigates intergenerational transmission and shifting performance spaces in Recife and Olinda. By analyzing community schools, carnival blocos, and heritage policies, it explores how institutionalization and urban change shape practices of continuity, adaptation, and local identity.

sections.name: Introduction and theoretical framework
sections.content:
1. Introduction and theoretical framework

Frevo—an exuberant, acrobatic fusion of fast-paced brass-band music, stylized dancing, and distinctive umbrella choreography—constitutes a central expressive form of Pernambuco’s carnival cultures and serves as a primary emblem of Recife and Olinda’s metropolitan identity. Historically circulated through rua (street) performance contexts—blocos, bandas, and neighborhood festas—frevo has in recent decades taken on a doubled life: continuing to reproduce as an embodied, ephemeral practice in street carnivals while simultaneously becoming the object of pedagogical labor, festival programming, museum display, and heritage management. This co-presence of street vitality and institutional inscription raises pressing questions about how frevo is transmitted across generations, how changing urban spatialities mediate transmission, and how cultural policy and institutional forms reconfigure continuities and ruptures in practice.

This article focuses narrowly on the interactions among three dimensions: modes of intergenerational transmission (familial, community-based, and institutional), the changing spatial arenas of performance (street routes, plazas, rehearsal halls, cultural centers), and the effects of cultural policy and heritage institutionalization in Recife and Olinda. By tracing how community schools of frevo, carnival blocos, and municipal/state heritage interventions produce particular regimes of learning, visibility, and legitimacy, the project aims to explicate the mechanisms through which institutionalization both stabilizes and reconfigures living tradition. The central research questions are: (1) In what ways do different transmission sites (street, community, institutional) produce distinct tecnical repertoires, pedagogies, and social relations for frevo? (2) How do processes of urban transformation in Recife and Olinda (route alterations, tourism infrastructure, gentrification of historic cores) redistribute opportunities for practice and apprenticeship? (3) How do heritage policies and institutional actors authorize particular versions of frevo and thereby shape continuity and change?

The theoretical framework integrates four analytical registers—performance theory, theories of tradition and institutionalization, spatial theory from urban studies, and frameworks on cultural transmission and pedagogy—to generate an empirically tractable conceptualization of frevo as a situated, embodied repertoire negotiated between street and institution.

1.1 Performance, embodiment, and repertoire
I employ performance theory (Turner; Schechner) to foreground frevo as an embodied repertoire constituted through situated enactment rather than as a static object. Performance theory directs attention to the cyclic interplay of practice, ritualized structure, and improvisation: the same musical phrase or umbrella gesture is meaningful only within recurrent social contexts that enable coordination, correction, and innovation. Relatedly, scholarship on musical and dance repertoires (Small; Nettl) emphasizes the distribution of knowledge across bodies, instruments, and social relations; this literature informs an analysis of how technical skills (rudiments of footwork, umbrella maneuvers, syncopated brass phrasing) are transmitted through embodied apprenticeship rather than solely through textual notation. Performance approaches also make it possible to trace how staged, institutional performances (concerts, school recitals) and improvisatory street enactments instantiate divergent criteria of competence and audience expectation.

1.2 Tradition, invention, and institutionalization
The literature on “invented” and “authorized” traditions (Hobsbawm & Ranger; Smith) and on cultural institutionalization provides a vocabulary to examine how frevo’s designation as heritage—municipal carnival emblem, state-recognized patrimony, and candidate for higher-level safeguarding—reshapes modes of authority and authenticity. Institutionalization entails processes of canonization (selection of standard repertoires, iconic choreographies), pedagogical formalization (curricula in community schools), and bureaucratic mediation (registration, funding, programming). Bourdieu’s concepts of field, habitus, and cultural capital are useful to analyze how institutional forms create new stakes (credentials, subsidy access, festival circuits) and how actors (mestres, directors, teachers, young practitioners) negotiate symbolic hierarchies. Institutionalization can stabilize transmission by providing resources and pedagogical infrastructures, but it can also produce exclusionary effects, standardize variants that were previously locally differentiated, and disembed practices from the situational ecology in which they developed.

1.3 Space, urbanization, and the production of performance arenas
Spatial theory—particularly Lefebvre’s production of space and Soja’s conceptualization of socio-spatial dialectics—frames frevo as inseparable from the urban forms that enable and constrain its circulation. Recife and Olinda present distinct urban morphologies and governance regimes: Recife’s ocean-front avenues and planned carnivalesque circuits provide different affordances from Olinda’s steep slope-streets, church-front squares, and UNESCO-recognized historic core. Changes in municipal planning, tourism-driven commodification of heritage areas, and localized processes of gentrification reconfigure where and when frevo can be performed, rehearsed, and taught. Spatial analysis thus links infrastructural and real-estate dynamics to shifts in apprenticeship patterns: the displacement of rehearsal spaces, the re-routing of bloco circuits, and the securitization or commercialization of public space affect not only access but the embodied timing and tempo of learning.

1.4 Cultural transmission, pedagogy, and communities of practice
To analyze how skills and knowledge move across generations, the framework draws on social learning theory and ethnographies of craft: Lave & Wenger’s “communities of practice” highlights legitimate peripheral participation as a mechanism by which novices acquire embodied competence through incremental involvement in routine activities. Applied to frevo, this lens interprets street-level participation in blocos and neighborly rodas as primary vectors of apprenticeship where children learn through observation, mimicry, and gradual entrustment. By contrast, institutional settings—community frevo schools, municipal workshops, conservatory programs—tend to formalize sequences of skill acquisition, introduce explicit pedagogical objectives, and use notation, standardized exercises, or graded ensembles. These divergent pedagogies produce different kinds of continuity: the street reproduces adaptive, context-sensitive repertoires; institutional pedagogy produces codified technique and documentation, facilitating circulation beyond local nodes but risking loss of localized improvisatory norms.

1.5 Heritage policy regimes and multiscalar governance
Finally, the framework situates cultural policy as a mediating layer that structures material and symbolic conditions for transmission. National agencies (e.g., IPHAN) and UNESCO-level frameworks shape discourses of safeguarding and provide instruments—inscription, funding lines, capacity-building—that alter incentives for community groups and municipal governments. Municipal and state cultural secretariats, festival organizers, and private stakeholders (sponsors, tourism operators) operationalize heritage at the local scale, selecting which practices are promoted and how resources are allocated. Drawing on policy studies of cultural governance, the analysis treats policies not as external overlays but as active producers of practice: they can encourage the institutional replication of frevo (support for escolas de frevo, performance circuits), foster marketization (ticketed events, branded products), or attempt to protect street-based modes through regulation and inclusive programming.

1.6 Analytical propositions and contributions
Synthesizing these registers yields four interrelated propositions that guide the empirical sections that follow:

- P1: Modes of transmission constitute distinct but intersecting ecologies—street-based apprenticeship, community-based collective transmission, and formal institutional pedagogy—each producing different technical repertoires, normative criteria of authenticity, and social hierarchies.

- P2: Institutionalization stabilizes repertoires and expands visibility and resource access, but also produces processes of selection and standardization that can displace locally conditioned variants and attenuate improvisatory competencies forged in street environments.

- P3: Urban spatial transformations reconfigure the topology of transmission: changes to performance routes, rehearsal infrastructures, and public-space governance reshape who learns, where, and under what temporalities.

- P4: Cultural policy mediates these dynamics by selectively authorizing particular versions of frevo; policy instruments can both support intergenerational continuity and create new dependencies and competitive logics that rework communal solidarities.

This section’s theoretical synthesis contributes to the field by offering an integrated model that links embodied transmission, spatial affordances, and policy-driven institutionalization. Rather than treating “heritage” and “street tradition” as opposed categories, the model treats institutionalization as a set of contingent transformations that coexist with—and are often sustained by—street practices. Empirically grounded analysis in Recife and Olinda can thus illuminate how local actors negotiate continuity and change, and how policies might support living transmission without flattening heterogeneity. The following sections operationalize this framework through ethnographic observation of escolas de frevo, participant observation in blocos, spatial mapping of performance circuits, and analysis of municipal and national heritage policies.

sections.name: Historical emergence and urban geographies of frevo in Recife and Olinda
sections.content:
2. Historical emergence and urban geographies of frevo in Recife and Olinda

This section maps the co-constitutive history and urban geographies that produced frevo as a distinct musical-dance formation in Pernambuco. Rather than offering a comprehensive chronological account, I focus on how specific social moments and built environments in Recife and Olinda shaped frevo’s stylistic grammar, modes of performance, and early practices of transmission. The argument proceeds in three parts: (1) the socio-historical conditions of emergence in late nineteenth–early twentieth century Recife; (2) differentiated urban morphologies and spatial practices of frevo in Recife; and (3) the contrasting topography and convivialities of Olinda and the implications for frevo’s form and circulation. Throughout I situate these developments within theoretical frames on the production of urban cultural space (Lefebvre), carnivalesque performance (Bakhtin), and embodied transmission (Bourdieu).

2.1 Emergence in Recife: social composition, sonic hybrids, and street practice

Frevo crystallized in Recife at the intersection of major social transformations at the turn of the twentieth century: the end of slavery and attendant reconfigurations of Afro-Brazilian urban life, rapid port-driven urbanization, and the institutional presence of military and civilian brass bands. In the dense working-class neighborhoods that surrounded the port and the historic center, popular Carnival practices — capoeira groups, pife (fife-and-drum) ensembles, bloco processions, and street dancers — converged with the sonic and formal resources of European-derived dance forms (polka, march) and municipal/military orchestras. The result was a hybrid musical idiom characterized by aggressive syncopation, compact melodic motifs, and an instrumental palette dominated by brass and percussion; concomitantly, the dance developed acrobatic, percussive corporeal techniques performed by passistas using the small umbrella as a kinetic prop.

Crucially, early frevo was a street-born practice: transmission flowed from older to younger participants through embodied apprenticeship in quotidian street settings — impromptu rodas, doorways, rehearsal walks — rather than through formal pedagogy. This apprenticing favored short-unit repertoires (breaks, themes, cadences) and high-density improvisational skills that could be picked up by observation and embodied imitation. The role of capoeira practitioners and other street-trained dancers in the invention of passista techniques has been emphasized in historiographies of frevo; regardless of specific genealogies, the salient point for urban analysis is that frevo’s emergent repertoire and pedagogy were adapted to low-infrastructure, highly socialized urban spaces.

2.2 Recife’s flat grid and the scaling up of carnival performance

Recife’s nineteenth- and twentieth-century urban morphology — comparatively flat coastal terrain, broadening avenues, and a growing network of streets radiating from the historic center — created material conditions that allowed frevo to scale from neighborhood rodas to mass processions. Two spatial features were particularly consequential.

First, the configuration of wide thoroughfares and open plazas in the central districts permitted brass-heavy orchestras and large bloco processions to circulate with relative ease. The sonic projection of brass bands benefits from linear routes and open nodes where sound can be projected and reconfigured; consequently, the expansion of organized blocos in the early-to-mid twentieth century, and later the growth of mega-blocos, is intelligible as a response to Recife’s infrastructural affordances. The transition from small street rodas to organized, temporally scheduled parades also entailed a shift in performative scale — repertory elements lengthened, orchestrations became denser, and choreography adapted to moving crowds. This scaling process favored more formalized, choreographed group practices and created incentives for collective organization (associações, blocos) that would later institutionalize teaching and rehearsal.

Second, the centrality of certain urban nodes — the port precinct, the Mercado and surrounding commercial streets, and neighborhoods contiguous with the historic center — produced cultural agglomerations in which frevo performers, instrument-makers, and patron networks co-located. Such agglomeration fosters rapid stylistic diffusion and the formation of repertorial canons. Equally important were the ways municipal regulation, policing, and modernization projects shaped where and when carnivalesque practices could occur: episodes of restriction or displacement produced new routings and incentivized institutional spaces (clubs, guild halls) as rehearsal venues.

An emblematic spatial outcome in Recife is the emergence of large-scale blocos that perform predetermined routes and times, concentrating thousands of participants. The creation and routinization of such macro-processions constitutes a territorialization of frevo at the urban scale: frevo ceases to be solely a neighborhood technique and becomes an event-oriented urban spectacle — a shift with direct consequences for intergenerational transmission, which increasingly includes formal rehearsal schedules, pedagogical hierarchies within blocos, and the production of printed/recorded repertoires.

2.3 Olinda’s hills, alleys, and the intimacy of movement

Olinda presents a contrasting urban logic. Its colonial-era topography — a compact historic center perched on steep hills, articulated by narrow cobbled alleys, staircases, and small public squares — produces different affordances for movement, sound, and spectator-performer relations. In Olinda, processional flows are fragmented by topography: bands and dancers negotiate abrupt vertical shifts, encounter thresholds at stairways, and perform at nodes that are inherently more intimate than broad urban avenues.

This geography favors small, mobile ensembles and situational performance practices. Frevo in Olinda often circulates as part of mixed carnivalesque itineraries that include maracatu, cavalhadas, and street theater; the resulting hybridizations emphasize interactive, improvisatory exchanges between performers and an intimate local public. Dance techniques in this setting privilege agility, spatial negotiation, and close-range engagement rather than the expansive, spectacle-oriented choreography seen in Recife’s large blocos. The umbrella of the passista functions as an instrument of both display and navigation in stair-bound contexts.

Moreover, Olinda’s touristification from the late twentieth century onward — the promotion of its colonial center as a heritage landscape — complicates local performance ecologies. The commodification of festival routes and the rising presence of non-local audiences condition performance rhythms and demand forms of bodily presentation tailored to spectator expectations. However, the material constraints of Olinda’s streets impose limits on the scale of commodified spectacle, thereby preserving certain neighborhood-centered modes of transmission that prioritize apprenticeship in situ over mass organization.

2.4 Comparative spatial logics and implications for transmission

Comparing Recife and Olinda highlights two spatial logics that have historically framed frevo’s development: Recife’s expansionary, avenue-oriented logic enabled massification, orchestration, and institutional forms of organization; Olinda’s constricted, vertical logic sustained intimate, hybridized, and itinerant performance practices. These differences have direct bearing on pedagogical modalities. In Recife, the urban environment incentivized the formation of collectives, regularized rehearsals, and the eventual creation of community schools and bloco-affiliated instruction to coordinate large numbers of performers. In Olinda, transmission has remained more situational, generationally bound, and embedded in polyvalent street encounters.

The geographic differentiation also mediates gendered and classed patterns of participation. Large blocos that occupy public avenues create entry points for a broad, heterogeneous public but also require forms of capital (instruments, costumes, organizational networks) that can mediate access. In Olinda, the more localized, neighborhood-based circulation of frevo facilitates continuity of familial and kinship-based transmission but can limit the visibility of peripheral practitioners in citywide narratives. These spatially inflected access dynamics anticipate later debates about institutionalization and heritage policy — debates to which the subsequent sections turn.

2.5 Conclusion: space as formative of frevo’s social life

Understanding frevo’s emergence requires attending to the mutual constitution of practice and place. Recife and Olinda furnished distinctive material ecologies that shaped frevo’s sonic-kinetic grammar, its modes of transmission, and its organizational forms. The flat, open avenues of Recife enabled scaling and formalization; Olinda’s stair-bound alleys preserved intimate, hybrid street practices. An urban-material lens thus reveals why frevo has always been both a local repertory transmitted through embodied mentorship and an urban spectacle capable of mass mobilization — a duality that conditions subsequent institutionalization and heritage-making. The next section explores how these spatial histories inform contemporary practices of teaching and the institutional arrangements that mediate intergenerational transmission.

sections.name: Mechanisms of transmission: families, community schools, and carnival blocos
sections.content:
3. Mechanisms of transmission: families, community schools, and carnival blocos

This section disaggregates the principal mechanisms by which frevo is learned, reproduced, and adapted in Recife and Olinda. It situates each mechanism within processes of embodied learning, socialization, and institutional mediation, and highlights distinct contributions and tensions that arise when movement, sound, and civic space intersect.

1. Families: early socialization, habitus, and normative repertoires
- Mode of transmission. Family-based transmission is primarily informal, relying on observation, mimicry, and embodied repetition. Children encounter frevo through domestic listening, radio, home rehearsals by relatives, and attendance at small family performances. Learning at this stage is tacit and sensorimotor: children internalize tempo, posture, footwork motifs (passadas), and basic musical phrases before receiving any formal instruction.
- Social functions. Familial transmission conveys not only technique but also the normative meanings of frevo: its relationship to neighborhood identity, Carnival obligations, and intergenerational prestige (who is a respected passista or mestre). Families mediate access to performance opportunities—introducing youth to local mestres, bloco leaders, or informal street sessions.
- Structure and inequality. The extent and character of familial transmission are stratified by class, gender, and migration. Households with a lineage of musicians or dancers provide dense, early exposure and social capital; households without such lineages often rely on external schools or blocos. Gender norms transmitted at the family level shape early role-taking (e.g., expectations about who should be a lead passista, who handles certain instruments), although these norms are actively contested in contemporary practice.
- Embodied memory and continuity. Families are crucial for preserving micro-variants—local step idioms, idiosyncratic arm movements, and neighborhood-specific repertoire—because intergenerational repetition ensures continuity at the level of habitus rather than codified technique.

2. Community schools: codification, inclusion, and professional pathways
- Institutional forms. Community frevo schools range from informal neighborhood ateliers run by a mestre to municipal- or NGO-supported programs offering regular classes, workshops, and certification. Pedagogies typically combine drill-based technical training (footwork sequences, brass phrasing, percussive patterns) with historical and theoretical components (history of frevo, Carnival logistics, instrument care).
- Pedagogical logic. Teaching in community schools synthesizes apprenticeship models with elements of formal schooling. Instructors scaffold learning through graduated tasks: isolation of movement elements, patterned repetition, ensemble synchronization, and staged performance. Schools often employ "cycle" pedagogy keyed to the Carnival calendar—intensive rehearsals culminating in public parade participation—thus aligning skill acquisition with ritual temporality.
- Social functions and outcomes. Community schools serve multiple social objectives: cultural transmission, youth inclusion, and workforce development (pathways into professional orchestras, cultural tourism, or teaching). They act as sites of gender inclusion: deliberate recruitment of girls and young women has shifted the gender composition of passistas and small ensembles, challenging traditional family-imposed roles.
- Tensions and trade-offs. Institutionalization introduces standardization: codified syllabi, assessment, and certification may increase mobility and recognition but can suppress local stylistic variants. Reliance on external funding (municipal grants, cultural foundations, tourism contracts) can orient curricula toward tourist-friendly repertoires and staged aesthetics, producing a repertoire that is performative rather than vernacular. There is also the risk of credentialing that displaces older forms of legitimacy (lineage, mestre recognition) with bureaucratic markers.

3. Carnival blocos: public pedagogy, apprenticeship in motion, and repertoire circulation
- Learning in situ. Blocos are primary sites of situated learning (sensu Lave & Wenger) where peripheral participation converts into full membership through repeated public practice. The bloco functions as an open classroom: novices learn timing, spatial navigation in dense crowds, ensemble listening, and improvisational responsiveness by performing alongside experienced musicians and dancers during actual parades.
- Ensemble dynamics and aural transmission. Frevo transmission within blocos emphasizes aural-oral methods—call-and-response cues, leader-led transitions, and micro-adjustments made in real time to tempo and phrasing. This yields high fidelity in ensemble coordination but also permits on-the-fly variation and local innovation. Blocos sustain repertoire circulation: songs and instrumental passages propagate across neighborhoods through repeated carnival cycles.
- Spatial and material pedagogy. The street imposes learning constraints and affordances—acoustics of open air, physical navigation among spectators, and the need for projection and endurance. These conditions shape technique (exaggerated arm gestures, steps adapted for uneven pavement) and impart situational knowledge (how to reposition an orquestra when a route is blocked, how to pace a two-hour stretch).
- Institutional hybridity. Some blocos are long-standing community entities (e.g., Galo da Madrugada in Recife) with layered institutional memory; others are ephemeral, tourist-oriented projects. Long-standing blocos function as custodians of specific repertoires and styles; newer blocos may hybridize frevo with other genres to appeal to broader audiences. Municipal regulations (permits, route approvals) and municipal support can privilege certain blocos, affecting who gains the pedagogical benefits of parade participation.
- Transmission of improvisation and risk management. Blocos are where improvisational skills are learned under risk—mistakes are public but learning is immediate. Senior members mediate this risk by step-instruction and by calibrating ensemble density, allowing novices to learn incrementally.

4. Interactions among mechanisms and emergent effects
- Complementarity and redundancy. Families, schools, and blocos operate in overlapping registers: families supply early exposure and normative framing; schools codify technique and broaden access; blocos provide situated, high-intensity practice. Together they form a resilient transmission ecology in which loss or weakening of one node (e.g., reduced family lineages) can be partially compensated by others (e.g., expanded school programs).
- Standardization versus variability. Institutionalization (through schools and heritage programs) tends to standardize form and repertoire, producing transmissible, teachable packages of movement and music. Street-based transmission in blocos resists total standardization because it privileges improvisation, neighborhood variants, and embodied adjustment to contingencies. This tension is central: institutional conservation stabilizes frevo for wider recognition, while street practice sustains adaptive capacity and local meaning.
- Generational recomposition. Younger practitioners socialized through schools and tourist-facing performances may prioritize visibility and technical polish, while older practitioners emphasize local idioms and ritual knowledge. This generational recomposition affects repertoire choices, costume aesthetics, and the valuation of different performative registers (stage vs. street).
- Policy feedback loops. Heritage recognition, municipal funding, and tourist demand create feedback loops that shape transmission: funding for schools increases formal training; heritage listings can legitimize curricular programs; but policy-driven priorities may channel frevo practice into staged, commodified forms. Conversely, strong bloco cultures can resist or reappropriate institutional initiatives by asserting neighborhood control over parade formats.

5. Metrics and indicators for assessing transmission efficacy
To analyze transmission across these mechanisms, useful indicators include:
- Intergenerational participation rates within families, schools, and blocos (age cohorts present).
- Repertoire fidelity and variation metrics (presence/absence of canonical frevo pieces; measured changes in tempo, phrasing).
- Frequency and intensity of public practice (hours per week of ensemble rehearsal; number of parade appearances).
- Institutional penetration (number of community schools, municipal programs, and officially sanctioned blocos).
- Gendered participation statistics and evidence of role change.
- Career trajectories (proportion of school graduates who join professional orquestras or become instructors).

6. Implications for continuity, adaptation, and policy
Mechanisms of transmission are not neutral conveyors of a fixed tradition; they are active shapers of what frevo becomes. Policy interventions that aim to safeguard frevo should:
- Support the plurality of transmission sites (sustain family-centered recognition, fund community schools, protect street parade spaces).
- Avoid narrow standardization that divorces technique from the embodied exigencies of street performance.
- Invest in curricular designs that combine motor skill training with contextual knowledge (Carnival logistics, neighborhood histories).
- Prioritize equitable access so that transmission does not reproduce existing inequalities in cultural capital.

Conclusion
Families, community schools, and carnival blocos constitute a complementary triad through which frevo is embodied, taught, and reconfigured. Each mechanism contributes distinct affordances: early tacit socialization (families), codified pedagogy and social inclusion (schools), and dynamic, situated learning under public pressure (blocos). Understanding their interactions—and the political-economic forces that reshape them—is essential for any intervention that seeks to conserve frevo’s continuity without impoverishing its capacity for local innovation.

sections.name: Heritage policy, institutionalization, and the festival economy
sections.content:
4. Heritage policy, institutionalization, and the festival economy

This section analyzes how heritage policy and the institutional apparatus that surrounds frevo intersect with the festival-driven economy of Recife and Olinda, and how those intersections reconfigure transmission, performance spaces, and local livelihoods. The argument proceeds in three linked parts: (1) the material and regulatory forms through which frevo has been institutionalized; (2) the economic and spatial dynamics of festivalization and tourism that both enable and constrain frevo’s reproduction; and (3) the resulting tensions and policy implications for safeguarding a living tradition while sustaining livelihoods.

Institutionalizing frevo: infrastructures, curricula, and museumification
State and municipal cultural policies, together with civil-society organizations, have produced a layered institutional infrastructure for frevo. This infrastructure includes dedicated cultural centers and museums (notably the Casa do Frevo in Recife), municipally funded community schools, formalized curricula for music and dance instruction, and programmatic funding streams for groups and events. Heritage recognition—at national and international levels—has supplied symbolic capital that facilitates access to public and private funds and legitimates preservation-oriented interventions.

Institutionalization alters modes of transmission in several concrete ways. First, the apprenticeship model embedded in street and bloco contexts is complemented and sometimes supplanted by classroom-style pedagogy: scheduled lessons, graded repertoires, and certified instructors. This produces greater technical diffusion and creates career pathways (teaching contracts, contracts for municipal programs), but it also narrows informal routes of knowledge transfer (on-the-street mentoring, familial transmission) and can privilege codified repertoires over improvised variants. Second, museumification—exhibitions, archival projects, and staged frevo shows—renders certain repertoires and iconographies more visible and thus more authoritative. Selection processes implicit in curatorial and curricular choices influence which tempos, choreographies, and instrumental lineages are valorized as “authentic,” with downstream effects on what younger practitioners learn and perform.

Festival economy and the spatial politics of performance
Frevo’s institutionalization is entwined with the commercial and civic logic of festivalization. Carnival and year-round carnavalized events are major economic drivers in Recife and Olinda: they mobilize public budgets, draw tourist flows, and generate income for musicians, dancers, street vendors, local bars, and the hospitality sector. Municipal planning increasingly treats frevo and related spectacles as assets within broader urban branding and creative-economy strategies.

This economic valorization produces asymmetric spatial outcomes. On the positive side, festival-driven investment can underwrite public infrastructure (sound systems, sanitation, lighting) and create paid performance opportunities. On the negative side, the commodification of frevo often privileges controlled, ticketed, or sponsored presentations—staged shows in theaters, curated performances in cultural centers, or corporately sponsored festa arenas—over open, improvisational street practice. Municipal permitting regimes, security protocols, and crowd-management measures that accompany large-scale festivals reconfigure street circuits, sometimes displacing traditional bloco routes or imposing temporal limits on informal gatherings. In historic precincts of Olinda and Recife, the festival economy can accelerate short-term rental markets and service-sector gentrification, raising costs for residents and altering the social mix that sustains street-based transmission.

Economically, institutionalization mediates income streams but does not eliminate precarity. Public contracts and festival fees create intermittent but higher-profile earnings for flagship groups and certified instructors, while myriad peripheral practitioners—drummers, young dancers, informal vendors—remain dependent on gig-based, weather- and calendar-dependent income. Sponsorships and cultural tourism revenues often flow through intermediaries (event promoters, municipal agencies, venue owners), and metrics used to justify funding (tourist numbers, ticket revenue) privilege quantifiable outputs over less tangible values such as intergenerational mentoring or noncommercial community gatherings.

Governance architectures and actor constellations
The governance of frevo is polycentric: municipal cultural secretariats, state agencies, national heritage institutions, non-governmental collectives, blocos, and private sponsors all play roles. Heritage frameworks that emphasize safeguarding introduce mechanisms intended to involve communities in decision-making, but in practice community influence varies. Larger, better-organized groups are more effective at navigating funding channels and bureaucratic requirements; smaller neighborhood ensembles may lack administrative capacity, reinforcing inequalities within the field of practice.

Public–private partnerships and market-oriented cultural policies contribute resources but also reorient priorities toward sellable formats. The rise of certified training programs and formalized professional pathways creates new status hierarchies among practitioners and can shift curricular attention toward marketable competencies (stage choreography, ensemble coordination, recording techniques) at the expense of the less remunerative but culturally central practices of street improvisation and spontaneous bloco formation.

Tensions: living heritage versus preservation and economic inclusion
Three core tensions emerge from the institutionalization–festival economy nexus. First, safeguarding as institutional preservation can constrict the dynamic, adaptive character of frevo by imposing fixed repertoires and staged performances that become models of “authenticity.” Second, festivalization and tourism can simultaneously energize frevo’s visibility and marginalize the everyday social contexts where transmission occurs, making the tradition increasingly dependent on cyclical, event-based economies. Third, economic and administrative barriers risk excluding the same communities most responsible for frevo’s vitality from both decision-making and economic benefit.

From an analytic perspective, these tensions are well captured by debates in cultural policy studies: the conflict between heritage-as-resource (usable for economic development) and heritage-as-practice (a living social process); the commodifying tendencies of festivalization; and the ways governance arrangements mediate whose cultural labor is recognized and remunerated. The conceptual lenses of cultural economy, heritage governance, and performative authenticity illuminate the mechanisms by which institutional forms reshape both practice and place.

Policy implications and pathways for equitable safeguarding
A policy stance that seeks to sustain frevo as a living practice while harnessing its economic potential should attend to four priorities:

- Support plural transmission pathways. Funding instruments should explicitly resource street-based apprenticeship, bloco-led mentoring, and informal pedagogies alongside formal schools. Small grants, stipends for bloco tutors, and flexible microfunding for neighborhood initiatives help preserve noninstitutional transmission channels.

- Decouple recognition from restrictive standardization. Heritage designations and museum programming should emphasize adaptive practices and document multiple local variants. Curatorial and curricular processes must be participatory, rotating which practitioners and repertoires receive visibility and resources.

- Redistribute festival revenues and access. Municipal contracts, sponsorship agreements, and ticketing policies should include requirements for inclusive hiring, local procurement, and revenue-sharing with neighborhood groups. Metrics for success must include community-level indicators (participation rates, local employment) in addition to tourist arrivals.

- Protect performance spaces within urban planning. Zoning, temporary-use permits, and infrastructure planning should safeguard traditional bloco routes and common streets as cultural commons, mitigating the effects of short-term rental-driven gentrification and ensuring that urban design facilitates, rather than fragments, spontaneous performance.

Conclusion
Heritage policy and festival economies have amplified frevo’s visibility and created new institutional supports, but they also reconfigure the social ecologies and urban geographies through which the tradition is transmitted. A critical policy orientation recognizes institution-building as necessary but not sufficient: safeguarding must be calibrated to sustain the informal, improvisational, and community-rooted practices that constitute frevo’s vitality, while distributing the economic benefits of festivalization more equitably. Future research and policy design should prioritize participatory governance experiments, evaluative frameworks that capture intangible outcomes, and spatial policies that protect the street as a living site of cultural transmission.

sections.name: Discussion: identity, continuity, and prospects for frevo’s future
sections.content:
5. Discussion: identity, continuity, and prospects for frevo’s future

This study has shown frevo to be simultaneously a practice of embodied knowledge, a set of spatialized performances, and an object of cultural governance. The empirical contrasts between Recife and Olinda—between community-led escolas de frevo, carnival blocos, municipal cultural centers, and heritage apparatuses—reveal continuity not as simple reproduction but as a negotiated, multi-scalar process. Below I synthesize three interlinked axes that structure frevo’s ongoing evolution (identity, transmission, and space-policy), identify key tensions exposed by the fieldwork, and outline targeted prospects for safeguarding practices that maintain both vitality and local agency.

1. Identity as practice and negotiation
Frevo’s identity is produced in performance and reproduced through situated social relations rather than residing in a static repertoire. Drawing on concepts of performative tradition and social practice, the data indicate that identity claims surrounding frevo are plural and contested: practitioners emphasize lineage and local styles (Recife’s virtuosic instrumentalism; Olinda’s street choreographies and giant figures), while municipal and heritage actors frame frevo as a singular, emblematic heritage to be preserved and promoted. These framings create distinct incentives. Community schools and blocos foreground embodied transmission, youth apprenticeship, and collective belonging; institutional recognition (municipal labels, UNESCO inscription) generates symbolic capital that can increase visibility and funding but also tends toward standardization and display-oriented performances.

Theoretical implications: rather than a dichotomy between “authentic” grassroots practice and “inauthentic” institutionalization (a binary critiqued in heritage studies), frevo should be read as a dynamic field in which multiple authenticity regimes coexist and compete. This aligns with Bourdieuian notions of cultural fields—actors negotiate symbolic and material capital—and with recent work on living heritage that emphasizes practice-based identity. Identity outcomes thus depend on who controls transmission channels and the spatial modalities in which frevo is enacted.

2. Continuity through multiple transmission ecologies
Intergenerational continuity in frevo operates through overlapping ecologies: familial apprenticeship, escola de frevo pedagogy, bloco participation, and mediated/digital learning. The fieldwork shows that escuelas de frevo are pivotal as institutionalized sites of learning that combine formal curricula (rudiments of technique, music theory) with informal mentoring, yet their curricularization risks narrowing repertoires and privileging performative showpieces over context-specific street choreographies. Blocos and street contexts remain critical for transmitting improvisational competence, situational awareness, and the social meanings of carnival performance.

Key tensions:
- Standardization vs. improvisation: institutional curricula facilitate measurable skills but may under-emphasize the improvisational, responsive competences learned in street contexts.
- Economies of transmission: reliance on municipal funding or tourist income can shift pedagogical priorities toward spectacle and marketable routines.
- Demographic change: youth engagement is robust where schools and blocos offer pathways to social recognition and micro-economies (paid gigs); conversely, where rehearsal spaces and funding are absent, youth migration and alternative leisure activities erode participation.

Prospect for continuity: safeguarding strategies should treat transmission ecologies holistically—supporting both school-based pedagogy and street-based apprenticeship—so that technical skill and contextual knowledge co-develop. This means curriculum design that embeds street practice modules, rotating residencies for seasoned bloco leaders in escolas, and apprenticeship stipends that make participation economically viable.

3. Spatial politics: street, stage, and urban change
Space is constitutive of frevo practice. The street is not merely a site where frevo is performed; it shapes timing, movement dynamics, and the social relations that sustain tradition. Urban interventions—heritage zoning in Olinda’s historic center, pedestrianization in Recife Antigo, noise ordinances, and tourism-driven commercialization—reconfigure these affordances. Two spatial dynamics stand out:

- Institutional shifting of performance into managed stages and cultural centers can increase safety and audience reach, but it removes key elements of the performance ecology (spontaneity, collective circulation, contested use of urban commons). Stages often reframe frevo as spectacle rather than communal practice.
- Urban redevelopment and gentrification constrain rehearsal and procession routes, reduce low-cost communal spaces, and can displace long-standing community networks. These processes disproportionately affect neighborhoods that have been frevo’s incubators.

Policy implication: spatial governance must prioritize the “right to the street” for cultural practices. This requires integrated urban-cultural planning that preserves procession corridors, protects informal rehearsal sites, and mediates tourism through community management rather than top-down commodification.

4. Institutionalization and cultural policy: risks and opportunities
Institutionalization—whether through municipal agencies, cultural centers, or UNESCO listing—creates resources and protection but also produces path dependencies. The research identifies four policy-relevant outcomes:

- Positive: institutional recognition attracts funding, enables infrastructure (sound equipment, rehearsal rooms), and legitimizes frevo in formal education and cultural tourism strategies.
- Negative: policy-driven standardization can privilege certain formations, marginalize hybrid or improvisatory practices, and instrumentalize frevo for economic development at the expense of community stewardship.
- Mediating variables: the distributional effects of policy depend on governance modalities—participatory, transparent policy processes favor community resilience; top-down, market-oriented policies favor spectacle and private profit.
- Gender and inclusion: institutional programs that do not explicitly address gender and class inequalities risk reproducing exclusionary patterns; conversely, targeted support (scholarships, leadership training) can significantly broaden participation.

Recommendation: cultural policies should operationalize safeguarding as adaptive governance—supporting plural transmission pathways, funding grassroots institutions directly, institutionalizing participatory management councils, and embedding monitoring with community-defined indicators of vitality.

5. Prospects and targeted recommendations
To sustain frevo’s vitality while respecting its plural identities, the following targeted priorities emerge from the analysis:

- Support hybrid transmission infrastructures: fund collaborative programs linking escolas de frevo, blocos, and municipal centers; create exchange residencies for senior practitioners; incorporate street-practice modules into formal curricula.
- Protect and plan urban commons: map and legally protect key procession routes and rehearsal spaces; require cultural impact assessments in redevelopment projects affecting frevo neighborhoods.
- Decentralize heritage governance: establish community-led heritage councils with decision rights over programming, festival scheduling, and revenue-sharing from tourism.
- Foster inclusive participation: fund initiatives that reduce barriers to entry (instrument loans, stipends), promote female leadership, and support Afro-Brazilian and peripheral neighborhood groups.
- Leverage digital tools responsibly: encourage community-owned digital archives and open-access pedagogies that complement, not replace, embodied learning; address digital divide issues.
- Monitor empirically: develop a concise set of indicators to track continuity (youth participation rates by age/gender/location), spatial access (number and diversity of rehearsal/procession sites), institutional dependence (share of funding from public vs. private/tourism sources), and repertoire diversity (presence of street vs. staged forms).

6. Concluding synthesis: continuity as adaptive pluralism
The future of frevo in Recife and Olinda is not a simple choice between preservation and change but a political-cultural negotiation over which forms are enabled, who benefits, and which spaces remain commons. Continuity will be robust where practices are supported as living ecologies: where schools, blocos, families, and municipal actors interact through participatory governance; where urban planning safeguards the performative capacities of streets; and where policy recognizes transmission as a socio-economic process requiring targeted support. Conceptually, this argues for reframing heritage safeguarding from static protectionism toward adaptive pluralism—policies and practices that accept heterogeneity, foreground intergenerational apprenticeship, and secure the material and spatial conditions that allow frevo to remain both rooted and inventive.

This reframing has implications beyond Pernambuco: it provides a model for intangible cultural heritage governance that centers practice, space, and agency simultaneously—an approach that can be operationalized through cross-sectoral policy instruments, localized monitoring, and sustained investment in the everyday infrastructures of performance.

It further frames frevo as a central expressive form of Pernambuco’s carnival cultures and as a primary emblem that signifies the metropolitan identities of Recife and Olinda.
